vignette:
Thomas, a 68-year-old European American politician, first came for help after months of feeling as if his life had shrunk to the space between his office, his home, and the few routes he believed he could still manage without catastrophe. The accident that changed him had happened late in the evening after a public event, when his car was struck hard at an intersection and spun with such force that, afterward, he could remember only a handful of vivid moments: the lurch of metal, the smell of alcohol on the breath of the other driver as rescue workers leaned in, the crushing impact against his ribs and shoulder, and the sight of two cars badly hit and twisted in the road. Those moments had stayed with him as separate pictures, and whenever they returned, they came with a blunt bodily certainty; he would feel pain in the same parts of his body, as if the crash were happening again inside him.

From the beginning, Thomas had found himself dwelling on what he had done wrong. He replayed the evening over and over, convinced that the sort of person he was—careful, responsible, used to making decisions for others—should have been able to prevent it. Every time he caught sight of a dented bumper in traffic or heard the metallic jolt of cars brushing together on the evening news, the thought arrived with it that he had failed in exactly the way a man like him should never fail. Those reminders did not just stir memory; they immediately hardened into the belief that the crash said something shameful and dangerous about him. That self-blame quickly became a habit of rumination, and it pulled his attention back to the event every time he tried to put it aside. He would start to explain what happened to his wife or a colleague, then lose the thread halfway through, his mind filling instead with the same broken fragments of memory. He noticed that the more he tried to account for it, the more the scene narrowed into those few pictures, each one bright with the sensation of pain. He came to believe that the accident had marked him in a way other people could somehow see, and he watched their faces for evidence that they could tell something had happened to him just by looking.

Those beliefs shaped his daily life. Because he was certain that the event reflected something defective in him, he felt he had to be on guard all the time, especially in public settings where he could not control what might happen or what people might notice. He had learned that keeping busy and keeping the television or radio on helped drown out the images; silence, especially at night, was when the memory got a foothold and came back in full, with the smell of alcohol and the violent jolt of impact attached to it. The more he tried to stay away from stillness, the more the accident remained close and unfinished in his mind. In the weeks after the crash he became alert to any unusual silence, and silence at night was the worst; if he woke and the house was quiet, he would check whether he was safe, listening for the smallest sound before letting himself settle again. The same sense of danger followed him into the day. At his age and in his role, he still had to move between meetings, constituency events, and city appointments, but he now avoided driving and often refused to be a passenger as well, leaving his staff to rearrange schedules around him. When he moved through a crowded parking garage or sat strapped into a car he did not control, the feeling that something terrible might happen again pulled the crash back toward him, as if his mind had to revisit those twisted cars and the crushing impact in order to stay alert. The threat did not stay in the present for long; it tipped him straight back into the evening of the accident. When he did have to ride in a car, the discomfort of being strapped in and unable to change the situation would set off the old images of crushed metal and the smell of alcohol, and with them the thought that he should have seen it coming, that he had somehow invited it by the kind of person he was.

The more he tried to push away the pictures, the more they returned. A smell of alcohol at a reception, or the sight of one car striking another on the evening news, would bring the accident back with surprising force, and those triggers were now enough to set off a chain of self-reproach and fear. He found that the harder he worked to keep those reminders at bay, the more abrupt and fragmented the memory became when it broke through anyway, stripped down to flashes of metal, pain in his ribs and shoulder, and the driver’s alcoholic breath. Avoiding the subject, avoiding the images, and avoiding the car had not emptied his mind of the event; it had kept the memory unprocessed and ready to intrude. He would begin by blaming himself again, then find his attention captured by the same snapshot memories, each one carrying a flash of bodily pain. Once the memory took hold, he became more watchful, scanning for signs of threat and feeling increasingly unable to concentrate on the work that had once defined him. Even a moment of discomfort in his body could send him back into the event, as if his own sensations were proof that the damage was still present.

By then, the effort to stay away from reminders had begun to feed the very thing he feared. He avoided the car, but that avoidance made every necessary trip feel more fraught, and each delay or rearranged appointment seemed to confirm that he was no longer fully capable. He avoided thinking about the crash, yet the gaps in his account made the memory return in fragments, less coherent and more terrifying than before. He told himself to remain vigilant, but that constant watchfulness left him exhausted and more alert to any cue—a sudden silence, the discomfort of a cramped seat, a whiff of alcohol—that might signal another disaster. Thomas was finally seeking help because he could see that the pattern was tightening around him: he was losing confidence in public, pulling back from travel, sleeping badly, and feeling that the accident was still announcing itself in his body and in the eyes of others. What he most feared was that he would never again feel ordinary safety; what he most hoped was to stop being ruled by the crash and to be able to sit in a car, sleep through the night, and return to his work without feeling that every moment might break open into the same few images.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows triggers leading to self-blame and fear, but it does not clearly state that the triggers themselves cause negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
The vignette describes avoidance and watchfulness, but it does not explicitly show those maladaptive strategies leading back to the traumatic memory.
The vignette says threat increases watchfulness and scanning, but it does not clearly state that threat brings back the memory.
The vignette presents avoidance and vigilance as responses to the crash, but it does not explicitly show them causing the traumatic memory to recur or fragment.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers leading to self-blame and fear, but it does not clearly state that the triggers themselves cause negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette describes avoidance and watchfulness, but it does not explicitly show those maladaptive strategies leading back to the traumatic memory.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette says threat increases watchfulness and scanning, but it does not clearly state that threat brings back the memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette presents avoidance and vigilance as responses to the crash, but it does not explicitly show them causing the traumatic memory to recur or fragment.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
